people.name: Tom Gitaa
body: In the mid-1990s a young Kenyan graduate in the Twin Cities began pulling together news from East Africa into a two-page summary for friends who wanted news from home. He called it Mshale, the Swahili word for "arrow." That small digest grew into what MPR News calls Minnesota's longest-running newspaper serving African immigrants.

Tom Gitaa's hometown is Mombasa, Kenya's port city on the Indian Ocean. He came to Minnesota for college and planned to go back. He earned a business degree from Metropolitan State University in St. Paul. A diversity visa then led to permanent residence and, later, U.S. citizenship.

In 2001 Gitaa moved the paper to a free monthly schedule, printed by ECM Publishers in Coon Rapids. By 2005 he was publishing full time. That same period brought personal loss: his wife was diagnosed with lung cancer, and he was widowed with two children. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Mshale returned to weekly publication to carry health information and community news. In 2022 it printed about 5,000 to 6,000 free copies a week, plus about 2,000 mail subscriptions.

He was also the original host of Talking Drum, a current-affairs show on the African Broadcasting Network, where he interviewed guests including Wangarĩ Maathai. He has chaired the Minnesota Multicultural Media Consortium and served as president of the board of Books for Africa. Metropolitan State's spring 2025 alumni notes list him as Mshale's founder, editor-in-chief and publisher.
keyFacts: Hometown: Mombasa, Kenya.
1990: Came to Minnesota for college; earned a business degree from Metropolitan State University.
Mid-1990s: Started Mshale as a two-page digest. Sahan Journal dates this to 1996.
2001: Turned Mshale into a free monthly.
2005: Became a full-time publisher.
2020s: Returned Mshale to weekly publication during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Original host of Talking Drum; former board president of Books for Africa.
people.connectToWork: When your agency has information to share, which community publishers have you actually read, and what would you ask them about reaching their readers before you buy an ad or send a release?

people.name: Thomas Nyambane
body: In May 2020, in the first frightening months of the COVID-19 pandemic, Kenyan Minnesotans learned that one of their elders had died. Dr. Thomas Nyambane, a retired college teacher, died on May 17, 2020, at 69. Mshale reported his death as the first reported death of a Kenyan in Minnesota from the virus. His friend Daniel Monari called him a uniter of the community.

Nyambane moved from Kenya to the United States in the 1980s. He and his wife, Alice, went first to Texas and then to Minnesota, where they raised three children. He earned a bachelor's degree at the University of North Texas, two master's degrees at the University of St. Thomas and a doctorate at Bethel University. He taught for many years at Hennepin Technical College and had been retired only a few years when he died.

Outside the classroom he was a community leader and a church elder at a Seventh-day Adventist congregation in Mounds View. He raised money for Books for Africa through the Minnesota Kenyan International Development Association. His friend told Mshale he worked to bring Kenyans in Minnesota together, especially those from Gusii, and to link Minnesota with Kisii County, once joining a delegation of Minnesota firefighters who went there to train their counterparts.

His son told Mshale and the Nation that four back surgeries and diabetes had left him more vulnerable to the virus. The family wanted to honor his often-stated wish to be buried in Kenya, but the closure of Kenya's airspace complicated those plans.
keyFacts: 1980s: Moved from Kenya to the United States.
Earned degrees at the University of North Texas, the University of St. Thomas and Bethel University.
Taught for many years at Hennepin Technical College.
Raised money for books for schools in Kenya.
May 17, 2020: Died of COVID-19 at 69.
people.connectToWork: When someone you serve has died, how would you ask the family about where and how they want to bury them, and what in your process would slow down plans that cross a border?

people.name: Bernard Lagat
body: At the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, Japan, Bernard Lagat won the 1,500 meters and then the 5,000 meters. According to Carnegie Corporation's Great Immigrants profile, he was the first athlete to win world titles at both distances. Team USA notes that the 1,500 gold was the first ever for an American in that event at the world championships. He had become a U.S. citizen only two years earlier.
Lagat was born on December 12, 1974, in Kapsabet, Kenya, and went to Kaptel Secondary School. Running carried him to the United States on a recruitment to Washington State University.

Running for Kenya, he won Olympic bronze in the 1,500 meters at Sydney in 2000 and silver at Athens in 2004. He became an American citizen on March 29, 2005, and went on to compete for the United States, for a total of five Olympic Games. At Rio in 2016, at 41, he was the oldest member of the U.S. track and field team and finished fifth in the 5,000 meters. Team USA credits him with eight world championship medals, five of them gold. After the 2010 indoor season he donated his bonus earnings to Haiti earthquake relief.
He made Tucson, Arizona, his home. As of October 2026 the University of Arizona's staff directory lists him as head cross country coach and assistant track and field coach.
keyFacts: December 12, 1974: Born in Kapsabet, Kenya.
2000 and 2004: Olympic bronze and silver in the 1,500 meters, for Kenya.
March 29, 2005: Became a U.S. citizen.
2007: Won world titles at 1,500 and 5,000 meters, for the U.S.
2016: Finished fifth in the Olympic 5,000 meters at 41.
Head cross country coach at the University of Arizona.
people.connectToWork: Where does a form or conversation at work make someone choose one country or one identity, and does your decision actually need that choice?

people.name: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o
body: From December 31, 1977, to December 12, 1978, Kenyan authorities held Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o without trial at Kamiti Maximum Prison, after a play he co-created in his own Gikuyu language was staged for village audiences. He later wrote about it in Detained: A Writer's Prison Diary. He decided that African writers should write in African languages. He was harassed for years after his release, and in 1982 he went into exile, first in Britain and then in the United States.

He was born in 1938 near Limuru in central Kenya. He grew up during British colonial rule and the Mau Mau independence struggle, which shaped his early novels, including Weep Not, Child and The River Between. His later work included Petals of Blood, Wizard of the Crow and Decolonising the Mind, a book on language, colonialism and culture.

In 2001 the University of California, Irvine appointed him Distinguished Professor and inaugural director of its International Center for Writing and Translation. In 2002 he was elected an honorary member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters. In 2004, after 22 years of exile, he returned to visit Kenya, where he and his wife, Njeeri, were brutally attacked. In 2009 the Daily Nation reported him among 14 contenders for the Man Booker International Prize. He died on May 28, 2025, in Georgia, at 87.
He is best described as a Kenyan writer who lived and taught in the United States for decades, not as a Kenyan American. We found no record of U.S. citizenship.
keyFacts: 1938: Born near Limuru, Kenya.
1977–1978: Detained without trial after his Gikuyu-language theater work.
1982: Went into exile.
2001: Appointed Distinguished Professor at UC Irvine.
2002: Elected honorary member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters.
May 28, 2025: Died in Georgia at 87.
people.connectToWork: Which language would someone choose for the most important conversation you will have with them, and have you asked, even when their English is fluent?

people.name: Wangarĩ Maathai
body: In 1960, a young woman from the central Kenyan highlands was one of about 300 Kenyans chosen to study in the United States through the "Kennedy Airlift," funded through the Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. Foundation. Wangarĩ Maathai went to Mount St. Scholastica College in Atchison, Kansas. In 1964 she earned a degree in biology there.

She was born on April 1, 1940, in Ihithe, in Nyeri District. She earned a master's degree at the University of Pittsburgh in 1966 and then returned home. In 1971 she received a PhD from the University of Nairobi and became the first woman in East or Central Africa to earn a doctorate.

In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement. It paid rural women to plant trees, which restored damaged land and gave women income and a public voice. It grew into a campaign for democracy and women's rights, and her activism brought her into conflict with the government of the day. After she was elected to parliament in December 2002, she was appointed assistant minister for environment.

In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace. She died of ovarian cancer in Nairobi on September 25, 2011.
Maathai was not a Kenyan American. She was a Kenyan who studied in the United States and returned home, so she belongs here as part of the ties between Kenya and U.S. colleges.
keyFacts: April 1, 1940: Born in Ihithe, Nyeri District, Kenya.
1964: Earned a biology degree at Mount St. Scholastica College, Kansas.
1971: Earned a PhD at the University of Nairobi.
1977: Founded the Green Belt Movement.
2004: First African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
September 25, 2011: Died in Nairobi.

people.name: Lupita Nyong'o
body: At the 2014 Academy Awards, a Yale School of Drama graduate in her breakthrough film role won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress. Lupita Nyong'o won for playing Patsey, an enslaved woman, in 12 Years a Slave, and The Standard in Kenya reported her as the first Kenyan to win an Oscar.

Nyong'o was born on March 1, 1983, in Mexico City. Her parents, Dorothy and Peter Anyang' Nyong'o, are Kenyan and were in political exile when she was born. The family returned to Kenya during her childhood, and her father later became a member of Kenya's Senate. She identifies as Kenyan-Mexican.

She came to the United States for college and earned a film degree at Hampshire College in 2003, then a master's degree at the Yale School of Drama in 2012. In February 2016 she starred on Broadway in Danai Gurira's Eclipsed, about women surviving the Liberian civil war, and earned a Tony Award nomination. In 2019 Simon & Schuster published her picture book Sulwe, about colorism and self-esteem, which became a New York Times best seller.
In September 2024 news reports said she had recently become a U.S. citizen and would vote for the first time in that November's election.
keyFacts: March 1, 1983: Born in Mexico City to Kenyan parents.
2003: Film degree, Hampshire College. 2012: Master's, Yale School of Drama.
2014: Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for 12 Years a Slave.
2016: Tony Award nomination for Eclipsed.
2019: Published the children's book Sulwe.
2024: Reported as having recently become a U.S. citizen.
people.connectToWork: Does a field on your form leave room for someone born in one country to parents from another, who lives in a third, and what happens to the record when it does not?

people.name: Paul Chelimo
body: On August 20, 2016, in the Olympic 5,000-meter final in Rio de Janeiro, a U.S. Army soldier crossed the line second behind Great Britain's Mo Farah. Paul Chelimo was briefly disqualified for a lane infringement. The ruling was overturned, and the silver medal was his.

Chelimo was born on October 27, 1990, in Iten, in Kenya's highlands. He came to the United States as a college recruit. He started at Shorter in Rome, Georgia, where he won NAIA national titles, and then transferred to the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, where he was twice the NCAA 5,000-meter runner-up. He enlisted in the U.S. Army in 2014 and served as a water-treatment specialist. That year he entered the Army's World Class Athlete Program, which lets soldier-athletes train full time and, as Track & Field News reported, gave him an accelerated path to U.S. citizenship.

He added a bronze medal in the 5,000 meters at the 2017 World Championships in London. On August 6, 2021, at the Tokyo Olympics, he won bronze in the 5,000 meters in 12:59.05, for his second Olympic medal.
keyFacts: October 27, 1990: Born in Iten, Kenya.
Ran for Shorter and UNC Greensboro.
2014: Enlisted in the U.S. Army; entered the World Class Athlete Program.
2016: Olympic silver in the 5,000 meters.
2017: World championship bronze.
2021: Olympic bronze in the 5,000 meters.
people.connectToWork: If a veteran's military and immigration records are tied together, what would your process need to ask so that a gap in one is not read as a problem with the other?

people.name: Kakenya Ntaiya
body: As a young girl in the Maasai village of Enoosaen, in southwestern Kenya, Kakenya Ntaiya was engaged to be married at age five. She made a bargain with her father: she would go through the coming-of-age ceremony expected of her only if she could keep going to school. She kept studying and won a scholarship to the United States. The University of Pittsburgh says she was the first woman from her village to attend university in the U.S.

With her village elders' agreement she went to Randolph-Macon Woman's College in Lynchburg, Virginia, and then earned a doctorate in education at the University of Pittsburgh. While still a doctoral student, she founded what is now the Kakenya Center for Excellence in her home village. The first school opened in May 2009 with a class of 30 fourth-grade girls, the first primary school for girls in Enoosaen. The organization, known as Kakenya's Dream, opened a second school in 2018 and runs two boarding schools along with programs to keep girls in school.

In April 2008 she received a Vital Voices Global Leadership Award. She was named a National Geographic Emerging Explorer in 2010 and a CNN Top Ten Hero in 2013, and the University of Pittsburgh gave her its Exemplary Leader Award in 2023.

Earned her undergraduate degree at Randolph-Macon Woman's College.
April 2008: Vital Voices Global Leadership Award.

Earned a doctorate in education at the University of Pittsburgh.

people.name: Aliphine Tuliamuk
body: On February 29, 2020, in Atlanta, a runner from a remote village in Kenya's Rift Valley won the women's race at the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials in 2:27:23. Aliphine Tuliamuk, seeded only tenth, had become an American citizen less than four years earlier.

She was born on April 5, 1989, and gives her hometown as Posoy, Kenya. ESPN reports that she grew up in the village of Kongelai, one of 32 siblings. She ran two seasons at Iowa State and then transferred to Wichita State University in Kansas, where she could study public health. By the end of her college career in 2013 she had been named a first-team All-American nine times. She stayed in the United States and became a citizen in April 2016.
She represented the United States in the Olympic marathon at the 2020 Games, held in 2021, about seven months after the birth of her daughter. An injury forced her to drop out at 20 kilometers.
keyFacts: April 5, 1989: Born in Kenya; hometown Posoy.
Ran at Iowa State and Wichita State; a nine-time All-American.
April 2016: Became a U.S. citizen.
February 29, 2020: Won the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials.
2021: Ran the Olympic marathon for the U.S., seven months after giving birth.
people.connectToWork: What might you assume about someone's family, region or background from the country on their paperwork, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: Mĩcere Gĩthae Mũgo
body: In the mid-1970s a Kenyan play called The Trial of Dedan Kimathi put the Mau Mau freedom fighter Dedan Kimathi back on trial, this time on stage and on his own terms. Mĩcere Gĩthae Mũgo co-wrote the play with Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o. It later had a ten-day run at the University of California, Irvine.

Mũgo was born on December 12, 1942, in Kariria, Kirinyaga, in central Kenya. Women in Academia Report says she was the top student at Limuru Girls' High School, then almost entirely white, and that she turned down a scholarship to Oxford for Makerere University in Uganda. She earned graduate degrees in Canada and became the first woman in East Africa to hold a PhD in literature. In 1978 she became dean of the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences at the University of Nairobi.

After the attempted coup of August 1982 led to a crackdown on university intellectuals, she was smuggled out of Kenya with her daughters. The family first settled in Canton, New York, where she taught at St. Lawrence University. From 1984 to 1992 she taught at the University of Zimbabwe. In 1993 she joined the Department of African American Studies at Syracuse University and taught there for 22 years, chairing the department from 2005 to 2008. She held dual citizenship in Kenya and the United States.

Her books include the poetry collection Daughter of My People, Sing! (1976) and the study African Orature and Human Rights. She died in Syracuse on June 30, 2023, after a long illness with multiple myeloma.
keyFacts: December 12, 1942: Born in Kariria, Kirinyaga, Kenya.
First woman in East Africa to hold a PhD in literature.
1976: The Trial of Dedan Kimathi published, co-written with Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o.
1978: Named a dean at the University of Nairobi.
1982: Forced into exile.
1993–2015: Taught at Syracuse University.
June 30, 2023: Died in Syracuse.
people.connectToWork: If someone's move to the U.S. was forced by politics, how would that change what you ask about their earlier work, credentials or family, and how you explain why you are asking?

people.name: Chapurukha Kusimba
body: In 2018 the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, one of the oldest honor societies in the United States, elected a Kenyan-born archaeologist as a Fellow. Chapurukha Kusimba had grown up in Kaptola, a village on the slopes of Mount Elgon in Bungoma County, western Kenya.

He went to Kaptola Primary, Kimilili Boys' School and Chesamisi High School, and earned a bachelor's degree in education at Kenyatta University in 1986. He interned at the National Museums of Kenya at Fort Jesus, the old Portuguese fort in Mombasa, and later worked there as a research scientist. A scholarship took him to Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, where he earned a master's degree and a PhD between 1987 and 1993.

He spent about two decades in Chicago, as a curator at the Field Museum of Natural History and a professor at the University of Illinois. From 2013 to 2019 he taught anthropology at American University. He then joined the University of South Florida as a distinguished professor. As of October 2026 its anthropology department lists him as a professor on the Tampa campus.
Kusimba studies the Swahili coast and the long history of African trade, technology and states. He has more than 100 publications.
keyFacts: Born in Kaptola, Bungoma County, Kenya, about 1962 going by his age in a 2020 article.
1986: Bachelor's in education, Kenyatta University.
1987–1993: Master's and PhD, Bryn Mawr College.
Curator at the Field Museum in Chicago.
2018: Elected a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
Professor at the University of South Florida.

people.name: Wangechi Mutu
body: On September 9, 2019, four bronze women took their seats on the Fifth Avenue front of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The niches in the museum's façade, completed in 1902, had stood empty for 117 years. Kenyan-born artist Wangechi Mutu filled them with The NewOnes, will free Us: four seated figures that rework the caryatid, the column-like female figure that carries the weight of buildings in Greek marble and West African wood.

Mutu was born on June 22, 1972, in Nairobi and grew up there. She went to Loreto Convent Msongari, and in 1989 she left Kenya for the United World College of the Atlantic in Wales on a scholarship. After a brief return home in 1991, she moved to New York City. She earned a BFA at Cooper Union in 1996 and a master's in sculpture at the Yale School of Art in 2000.

She first became known for collages that combine magazine images, paint and found materials into strange, beautiful female figures. They raise questions about gender, race, colonial history and the environment. Her work is held by the Museum of Modern Art and the Brooklyn Museum. In 2010 Deutsche Bank named her its first Artist of the Year. Her first U.S. survey, A Fantastic Journey, opened at Duke's Nasher Museum of Art in March 2013 and traveled to the Brooklyn Museum. In 2023 the New Museum in New York presented Intertwined, a major survey of her work.
Her gallery says she lives and works between Brooklyn and Nairobi. It also shows her work at the Venice Biennale and the New Museum in 2026.
keyFacts: June 22, 1972: Born in Nairobi, Kenya.
1996: BFA, Cooper Union. 2000: MFA in sculpture, Yale.
2010: Deutsche Bank's first Artist of the Year.
2013: First U.S. survey, A Fantastic Journey.
2019: The NewOnes, will free Us, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
2023: New Museum survey, Intertwined.

people.name: Sally Kipyego
body: On February 29, 2020, at the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials in Atlanta, Sally Kipyego finished third in 2:28:52 and earned a spot on the U.S. Olympic team. Eight years earlier she had won an Olympic silver medal for Kenya.

She was born on December 19, 1985, in Kapsowar, in Kenya's Rift Valley highlands. She ran for Texas Tech University, where USA Track & Field reports that she was the first Kenyan to win an NCAA individual cross country title and the first woman in Division I to win three straight NCAA cross country titles. She also won six NCAA track titles. She earned a nursing degree at Texas Tech in 2009 and signed with Nike soon after. In 2019 Texas Tech named her to its Hall of Fame class.

Running for Kenya, she won silver in the 10,000 meters at the 2011 World Championships in Daegu and again at the 2012 London Olympics. She became a U.S. citizen in January 2017 and was cleared to compete for the United States in August 2019. At the Tokyo Games, with the marathon run in Sapporo in 2021, she finished 17th for Team USA.

Won nine individual NCAA titles for Texas Tech.
2009: Earned a nursing degree at Texas Tech.
2011 and 2012: World and Olympic silver at 10,000 meters, for Kenya.
January 2017: Became a U.S. citizen.
2021: Finished 17th in the Olympic marathon for the U.S.

people.name: Mũkoma wa Ngũgĩ
body: In 2009 a short story called "How Kamau Wa Mwangi Escaped into Exile" was shortlisted for the Caine Prize for African Writing. Its author, Mũkoma wa Ngũgĩ, was building a career as a novelist, poet and scholar in the United States.

He was born in 1971 in Evanston, Illinois, and raised in Kenya. He came back to the U.S. for his education: a BA at Albright College, an MA in creative writing at Boston University, and a PhD in English at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. As of October 2026 Cornell University's Department of Literatures in English lists him as a professor.

His novels include Nairobi Heat, Black Star Nairobi, Mrs. Shaw and Unbury Our Dead With Song. He has also published poetry and the study The Rise of the African Novel: Politics of Language, Identity, and Ownership (2018). In 2013 New African named him one of the 100 most influential Africans. He co-founded the Mabati-Cornell Kiswahili Prize for African Literature, which rewards writing in an African language. He is a son of the writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, also on this page.
keyFacts: 1971: Born in Evanston, Illinois; raised in Kenya.
2009: Shortlisted for the Caine Prize.
2018: Published The Rise of the African Novel.
Professor at Cornell University; co-founder of the Mabati-Cornell Kiswahili Prize.

people.name: Dennitah Ghati
body: In 2013 Dennitah Ghati was elected Women's Representative for Migori County in Kenya's National Assembly. In March 2014 a car accident in Nairobi injured her spine, and she has used a wheelchair since. From 2017 to 2022 she returned to Parliament as a nominated member representing persons with disabilities, and she was Vice Chairperson of the Kenya Disability Parliamentary Association.

Ghati holds an MSc in Social Work and International Affairs from Columbia University, funded by a Ford Foundation International Fellowship. In 2017 she founded the Dennitah Ghati Disability Foundation, which supports disabled adults and children, particularly at the grassroots level. She represented Kenya at the first Global Disability Summit in London in 2018. In September 2021 the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association named her Chairperson of its Commonwealth Parliamentarians with Disabilities network.
She is Kenyan, not Kenyan American; she studied in the U.S. Parliament's records show her term ended in August 2022. We did not find a later public office.
keyFacts: 2013–2017: Women's Representative for Migori.
March 2014: Spinal injury in a car accident; uses a wheelchair.
2017–2022: Nominated member of Parliament representing persons with disabilities.
2017: Founded the Dennitah Ghati Disability Foundation.
September 2021: Named Chairperson of the Commonwealth Parliamentarians with Disabilities network.
people.connectToWork: When you picture a disabled person from another country, who do you picture, and how would it change your conversation to assume they may know their rights and the law better than you do?

institutions.name: Mshale
body: Mshale started in the mid-1990s as a two-page digest of East African news. Tom Gitaa, a Kenyan who had come to Minnesota for college in 1990, mailed it to friends and acquaintances. By Sahan Journal's account, in its early days Gitaa printed it weekly at a Kinko's in Roseville, about 1,500 copies at a time.

In 2001 Mshale became a free monthly, printed on newsprint by ECM Publishers in Coon Rapids. As the internet made African news easy to find, the paper shifted toward local coverage of Minnesota's African immigrant communities. During the COVID-19 pandemic it went back to weekly publication, supported in part by Minnesota Department of Health outreach contracts. In 2022 it printed 5,000 to 6,000 free copies a week, had about 2,000 mail subscribers, and ran Mshale.com with two full-time staff and several freelancers. MPR News calls it Minnesota's longest-running newspaper serving African immigrants.
keyFacts: Mid-1990s: Founded by Tom Gitaa as a two-page news digest.
2001: Became a free monthly.
2020s: Returned to weekly publication during the pandemic.
2022: Printed 5,000 to 6,000 free copies a week, plus about 2,000 mail subscriptions.
institutions.connectToWork: If you paid a community paper to carry public health or benefits information, how would you learn whether it reached the people you meant to reach?

institutions.name: Kenyan Community Seventh-day Adventist Church
institutions.location: 6625 Humboldt Avenue North, Brooklyn Center, Minnesota
body: The church says its name comes from its Kenyan Adventist co-founders in 1998 and that it is open to and serves "people from every tribe and nation." It worships on Saturdays. Its programs include community care, Bible study and regular events.

In a first-person account from November 2024, Mshale's publisher Tom Gitaa, who is not an Adventist, called it "the premier house of worship for the Kenyan community" and the first Kenyan church in Minnesota to buy its own building. He described its congregation as Black Kenyan immigrants and wrote that he had sent visiting Kenyan officials there, and that about two years earlier it hosted the Kenya Embassy's largest mobile consular operation in the state. The same article names Simeon Mokaya Momanyi as pastor since about 2021.

The building shares a property line with the Brooklyn Center police station. By Gitaa's account, the church became a refuge for protesters fleeing tear gas after a Brooklyn Center officer killed Daunte Wright in 2021.

Gitaa's article was prompted by a dispute on October 26, 2024, when a member threw away copies of Mshale in the church parking lot. The pastor apologized and said no church policy bars the paper. It is one person's account, and a reminder that a congregation is not of one mind.
keyFacts: 1998: Founded.
Worships on Saturdays.
By Mshale's account, the first Kenyan church in Minnesota to buy its own building.
Has hosted a Kenya Embassy mobile consular operation, by Mshale's account.
institutions.connectToWork: Which days do your appointments, trainings and community meetings assume people are free, and who told you that works for them?

institutions.name: Minnesota Kenyan International Development Association
body: The Minnesota Kenyan International Development Association (MKIDA) is a small Minnesota nonprofit focused on Kenya. Its stated mission is to improve education, health and economic development in rural Kenya, and it calls education "the most powerful tool" for literacy and empowerment.

Its main project, Rural Kenya Books, collects books, and money for shipping, for rural schools in Gusii, western Kenya. MKIDA received federal tax-exempt status in November 2004. It works with Books for Africa in St. Paul: by June 2015 it had shipped four containers of books to the region, and that month the two groups sent a fifth container of about 22,000 textbooks to Kisii in memory of Ishmael Gitaa, father of Mshale's founder, to benefit more than 22 schools in Nyamira and Kisii counties. It has also held annual conferences that honor Kenyan graduates in Minnesota, such as one at the Maple Grove Community Center in July 2006. Its latest IRS filing we found is the short postcard for 2023, used by groups with gross receipts under $50,000, and its former web address no longer works.
keyFacts: November 2004: Granted federal tax-exempt status.
Main program: Rural Kenya Books.
June 2015: Fifth book container sent with Books for Africa.
2023: Filed IRS Form 990-N.

institutions.name: Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities
aliases: MN Community of African People with Disabilities
body: The organization says it was founded in 2014 by two physically disabled East African Americans in Minnesota who saw a need for services addressing language, cultural and social barriers. Its site says its mission is to enrich the lives of disabled African people, and lists basic and intensive support services, life skills, employment and day support.

A 2018 profile by the charity MATTER names Nimo Ahmed, who came to the U.S. from Somalia as a young child, as a founder and executive director, and describes outreach to disabled people in Somalia. A 2017 Minnesota Senate bill, SF 1959, as introduced, proposed $250,000 a year for fiscal years 2018 and 2019 for "supporting Somali and East African persons with disabilities." We did not establish whether it passed.

We found no Kenyan-specific disability organization in Minnesota. Nothing we read documents this organization serving Kenyan families in particular, so ask the organization and the person before suggesting it.
keyFacts: 2014: Founded in Minnesota.
Founded by disabled East African Americans, by its own description.
Documented work is mainly with Somali and East African people.
institutions.connectToWork: When no organization exists for a person's exact community, how would you offer a nearby option without assuming it fits, and what would you ask them first?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. We did not find a study of Kenyan immigrant families in Minnesota or anywhere in the U.S. Most of what follows comes from one study in one rural coastal county of Kenya, which cannot speak for a country with many ethnic groups, several faith traditions and large differences between cities and the countryside, or for anyone in Minnesota. Treat it as possibilities to ask about, not expectations.
questions: What do you call this at home, and in what language?
What words would you like me to use?
What have you or your family already tried, at clinics, at church or elsewhere, and what helped?
Who do you want involved in decisions and meetings, and is there anyone you do not want there?
Do you belong to a church, women's group or community association that you would like connected to your plan?
Which language do you prefer for sensitive topics, and would you like a professional interpreter?
Is there anyone you would not want interpreting for you, because of who they know?
Has anyone given you or your child a label or diagnosis? Who gave it, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
You do not have to answer this, but is there anything you would like me to know about how this began?
Could you tell me the next steps in your own words, so I can check that I explained them well?

context.heading: What one study in Kenya heard about explanations
body: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley (2017) ran 21 focus groups with 263 community health workers and women's group members in Kilifi County on the Kenyan coast, mostly among Mijikenda (Giriama and Chonyi) communities. Participants rarely gave a single cause. They often combined moral or family explanations, supernatural ones, religious ones such as God's will, and biomedical ones such as malaria, polio, birth complications and accidents. The authors suggest this mix can be read as "healthy pluralism": an active effort to make sense of a situation and improve it, rather than confusion.
How far this applies to anyone in the U.S. has not been studied. Variation by generation, faith, region and education should be expected, but no source we found measured it.

sources.label: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley, PLoS One (2017)

context.heading: Caregiving, blame and support
body: In the Kilifi study, mothers carried most of the caregiving and were also the people most often blamed. Caregivers described physical, emotional and financial stress, especially when combining care with paid work. Do not ask about cause in a way that could sound like blame, especially toward mothers. If cause matters for services, say why you are asking.
The same study took place inside existing women's groups and community health worker networks, which are community structures through which information and support already move.

sources.label: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley, PLoS One (2017)

context.heading: Stigma and disclosure
body: The Kilifi study documented serious stigma in some households. Children were hidden, restrained, kept home from school or blamed for household problems, and people who helped them sometimes faced stigma too. These findings come from one county and describe what participants reported. They are a reason to make it safe to talk, and say nothing about whether stigma exists in the home of the person you are meeting.

sources.label: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley, PLoS One (2017)

context.heading: Healers, faith and formal services
body: In the Kilifi focus groups, what a family might do was linked to how the disability was explained: a health explanation might lead to a medical centre, and an explanation of wrongdoing or an evil force might lead to a local witchdoctor. The authors write that it was common for two or more explanations to run at once, and one participant described a child taken both to hospitals and to church for prayers. They also write that when one course of action failed, that seemed to trigger a shift to another, and that it is possible pragmatism lies at the centre of these beliefs. Plan services that can sit alongside faith and community support when the person wants that.

sources.label: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley, PLoS One (2017)

context.heading: Language and interpreters
body: In Swahili, the words for deaf, blind and physically disabled people, kiziwi, kipofu and kilema, belong to a noun class other than the usual one for people. Many people read this as a sign of contempt. A 1997 article by Abel Y. Mreta disputes that reading, and the debate is unresolved. Kenyans also speak many other languages, and we found no source on which disability terms are preferred or stigmatizing in them, so use the person's own words.

Do not assume English is the right language for a sensitive conversation because someone speaks it fluently. Offer a professional interpreter, and check before using a community member, because of privacy in close networks.

sources.label: Mreta, Kiziwi, Kipofu na Kilema: Ubaguzi au Heshima? (1997), University of Dar es Salaam repository

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no study of how Kenyan Americans or Kenyan Minnesotans understand disability, nothing on who makes decisions in Kenyan American households, and nothing on immigration fears or trust in U.S. systems among Kenyan Americans in particular. We also did not find a Kenyan American disabled leader or advocate from Minnesota with enough public record to profile here. None of this means there are none. Ask the person, and do not fill the gap with assumptions.

sources.label: Bunning, Gona, Newton and Hartley, PLoS One (2017)

communityRoutes.name: Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities (MNCAPD)
communityRoutes.purpose: A Minneapolis nonprofit founded by disabled East African Americans. It lists support services, life skills, employment and day support. Its documented work is mainly with Somali and East African people, so ask whether it fits before suggesting it.

communityRoutes.name: Embassy of the Republic of Kenya, Washington, D.C.
communityRoutes.purpose: Consular help for Kenyan nationals, including passports, ID cards, birth certificates for children born abroad and transporting the remains of a person who has died. Useful when identity documents stand between a person and a service.

organizations.intro: Mshale's publisher uses the term "the Big Five" for the five largest African communities in Minnesota: Somalis, Ethiopians, Liberians, Kenyans and Nigerians. Numbers vary. In 2024 a festival organizer told Mshale there are about 10,000 to 15,000 Kenyans in Minnesota, and in 2025 Mshale, citing 2023 Minnesota Compass data, reported just over 20,000 immigrants with Kenyan origins. These are different measures from different dates, and neither is a count to plan services by. Mshale's reporting describes the northwest suburbs of the Twin Cities as a hub. This list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Mwanyagetinge
entries.purpose: Mshale calls it the largest organized group of Kenyans in Minnesota, drawing members from the Abagusii community, and in 2023 described it as almost four decades old. Members elect its officers. It helped organize Kenya Fest in Brooklyn Center in 2024. We did not find its own website.

entries.name: Kenyan Women in the United States (KWITU), Minnesota chapter
entries.purpose: KWITU's site lists a Minnesota chapter among its state chapters. The national organization held its 10th-anniversary convention in St. Paul in August 2025, with panels on domestic violence, women's health, financial literacy and entrepreneurship.

entries.name: Association of Kenyans in America (AKIA)
entries.purpose: Named by Mshale as a co-organizer of Kenya Fest, the 2024 Madaraka Day festival in Brooklyn Center. We did not find its own website.
entries.linkLabel: Mshale report on Kenya Fest 2024 (archived copy)

entries.name: Global Fatherhood Foundation
entries.purpose: Founded by Sam Mwangi. Its site offers fatherhood resources, workforce training and adult support services, and links to immigration legal services. Mshale named it a co-organizer of Kenya Fest in 2024.

entries.name: Minnesota Swahili Christian Congregation
entries.location: Minneapolis, at Holy Trinity Lutheran Church
entries.purpose: A Lutheran worship service in Swahili on Sundays at 12:00 p.m. Its host church says it welcomes all Swahili speakers and people from East African countries, and that its pastor is originally from Tanzania. A 2022 member profile says it uses Tanzanian Kiswahili.
entries.linkLabel: Holy Trinity Lutheran Church, partners page

entries.name: African Rhythms
entries.purpose: A Sunday show from 12 to 2 p.m. with Salif Keita and George "Jojo" Ndege, playing music from Africa and beyond. Ndege also organized Kenya Fest in 2024.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: A nonprofit newsroom founded in 2019 covering Minnesota immigrants and communities of color, including African communities. Not specific to Kenyans.

entries.name: Kenyan Women in the United States (KWITU)
entries.purpose: Founded in 2015 by Lilly Richards to help newly arrived Kenyan women. Says it works to "connect, support and empower" through mentorship, leadership development and community engagement. Mshale reported in 2025 more than 30 chapters and more than 14,000 members, and called it the largest organization of Kenyan women in North America. KWITU’s own chapters page lists 23 established state chapters and "12,000 plus members."

entries.name: Embassy of the Republic of Kenya, Washington, D.C.
entries.purpose: Consular services for Kenyans in the U.S., including passports, ID cards, birth certificates for children born abroad, emergency travel documents and transporting remains. Its site has a diaspora section with a page of diaspora organizations.

entries.name: State Department for Diaspora Affairs, Kenya
entries.purpose: Part of Kenya's foreign ministry. Its site offers a check on recruitment agencies, job placement information and help for Kenyans abroad.

entries.name: Kenya Community Development Foundation (KCDF)
entries.purpose: A public charitable foundation in Kenya, started in 1997, supporting community-driven development.

entries.name: Friends of KCDF-US
entries.purpose: A U.S. 501(c)(3) created to engage the Kenyan diaspora and give U.S. donors a way to fund development causes in Kenya through KCDF.

entries.name: Kenya Diaspora Alliance USA (KDA-USA)
entries.purpose: A nonprofit registered since 2016 that says it works to unite Kenyans in North America on civic and development issues, including the diaspora's right to vote.

entries.name: North American Kenyans Association (NAKA)
entries.purpose: Says it offers Kenyans in North America networking, mentorship, events and practical guides, including a guide on dual citizenship dated August 2026.

entries.name: The Standard
entries.purpose: National Kenyan and world news from The Standard Group, which also runs KTN, BTV and Radio Maisha.

entries.name: KTN News
entries.type: Television, with a live stream online
entries.purpose: A Kenyan TV news channel from The Standard Group that can be streamed through the Standard site.

entries.name: Citizen TV and Citizen Digital
entries.purpose: A Kenyan news brand from Royal Media Services, in English and Swahili, with news and live broadcasts online.

entries.name: Daily Nation
entries.purpose: A Kenyan daily first published in 1960, from the Nation Media Group. Its news site is at nation.africa.
